title: Permian–Triassic mass extinction
summary: About 251.9 million years ago, within roughly 60,000 years, most marine species and many land plants and animals died out: Earth's most severe known mass extinction, most likely set off by Siberian Traps magmatism and the warming it drove.
card: The end-Permian extinction, often called the Great Dying, is dated at Meishan in southeast China to between 251.941 and 251.880 million years ago. Gases from the Siberian Traps, above all from magma sills baking carbon-rich basin sediments, are the leading suspect, with warming, oxygen loss and ocean acidification doing the killing. Recent estimates put marine species loss near 81%, lower than the 90–96% long quoted.
what:
The Permian–Triassic (end-Permian) mass extinction is the largest loss of life in the Phanerozoic fossil record and the event that closes the Paleozoic Era. Its best-dated record is the Meishan section in Changxing County, Zhejiang Province, China, where volcanic ash beds interleaved with marine limestones and mudstones have been dated by uranium–lead (U-Pb) analysis of zircon crystals. Burgess and colleagues (2014) placed the onset of extinction at the base of Bed 25, 251.941 ± 0.037 million years ago (Ma), and the end of the main extinction interval at Bed 28, 251.880 ± 0.031 Ma, a duration of about 61,000 ± 48,000 years. The formal Permian–Triassic boundary, defined by the first appearance of the conodont Hindeodus parvus at the base of Bed 27c and ratified as a global stratotype in 2001, falls inside that interval at 251.902 ± 0.024 Ma, the age shown on the International Chronostratigraphic Chart (v2024/12).

A sharp drop in the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12 in marine carbonate, starting roughly 60,000 years before the die-off, records a large injection of isotopically light carbon into the ocean and atmosphere, and tropical sea-surface temperatures rose by about 10 °C. The prime suspect is the Siberian Traps, a large igneous province in northern Asia whose lavas, ash and intrusions total roughly 2–5 million km³. Lavas began erupting about 300,000 years before the extinction, but the extinction's onset matches the start of widespread sill intrusion into the sedimentary rocks of the Tunguska Basin.

Marine animals bore the brunt: heavily calcified organisms and species living far from the tropics were hit hardest. Estimates of the toll depend on method. The widely repeated figure of 90–96% of marine species comes from rarefaction work of 1979–1986; Stanley (2016), after separating out the earlier end-Guadalupian crisis and background extinction, estimated about 81% of marine species and 62% of genera. Whether the land extinction was simultaneous is also debated, because a 2020 date from South Africa's Karoo Basin places the classic vertebrate turnover there more than 300,000 years before the marine event.

uncertainty.note: 2-sigma analytical (internal) uncertainties from U-Pb zircon CA-ID-TIMS dates at Meishan (Burgess et al. 2014); tracer-calibration (0.03%) and U-238 decay-constant (0.05%) systematic uncertainties are additional. Duration 61 ± 48 kyr (abstract rounds to 60 ± 48 kyr). Carbon-cycle volatility continued for at least 500 kyr after onset.

paleo.plate_model: MERDITH2021 (Merdith et al. 2021, Earth-Science Reviews 214:103477) via GPlates Web Service
paleo.note: Meishan point reconstructed to 252 Ma. PALEOMAP gives 17.17° N, 103.88° E (about 1.6° of latitude and 1.5° of longitude from MERDITH2021). MULLER2019 covers only 0–250 Ma; at its 250 Ma limit it gives 25.14° N, 91.50° E versus MERDITH2021 19.03° N, 101.84° E, a spread of ~6° latitude and ~10° longitude that reflects differing absolute reference frames. For the Norilsk point at 252 Ma: MERDITH2021 61.85° N, 35.38° E; PALEOMAP 53.46° N, 36.49° E.

how: The favoured chain runs from magma to dead oceans. (1) Siberian Traps magmatism began with explosive eruptions and then floods of lava; this first, lava-dominated stage, about two-thirds of the lava volume (more than 1 million km³), started just before 252.24 ± 0.1 Ma and caused little measurable disruption of the carbon cycle. (2) At 251.907 ± 0.067 Ma, overlapping the extinction onset within uncertainty, eruption largely gave way to the intrusion of sills across more than 1.5 million km² of the Tunguska Basin; their heat cooked evaporite, carbonate and hydrocarbon-bearing sediments and probably released very large volumes of carbon dioxide and methane. Burgess and Bowring judged this contact-metamorphism model the most plausible, and found the plume thermal-erosion and nickel-fed methanogen hypotheses less consistent with the timing. (3) The rapid release of isotopically light carbon produced the carbon-isotope excursion and greenhouse warming of roughly 10 °C in tropical surface waters. (4) Warmer water holds less oxygen while animals need more: an Earth-system model reproducing the proxy record depletes global marine oxygen by almost 80%, leaves about half the seafloor anoxic, and implies that temperature-dependent hypoxia accounts for more than half the extinction's magnitude, worst at high latitudes. (5) Boron-isotope pH records show stable pH during a first phase of slow carbon input, then an abrupt acidification during a second, rapid carbon pulse that removed heavily calcified species. (6) Carbon-cycle instability lasted at least 500,000 years, and Siberian magmatism continued for at least 500,000 years after the extinction.
why_it_matters: This extinction closes the Paleozoic Era: the base of the Triassic, defined at Meishan, is also the base of the Mesozoic, so the familiar sequence of Earth's eras turns on it. By removing roughly four in five marine species and around three in five marine genera, it reset ocean ecosystems, and the Triassic world that followed was rebuilt from a minority of surviving lineages, including the conodonts whose first appearance now marks the boundary. On land, the Gondwanan glossopterid floras and the Daptocephalus fauna gave way to new assemblages, although the exact timing of that change is still argued. The event also matters as the clearest test in the rock record of what happens when large amounts of carbon enter the atmosphere quickly. Its dating shows that the killing was a matter of tens of thousands of years, not millions, and its mechanism links greenhouse warming to oxygen loss and acidification in the sea. Penn and colleagues explicitly connect it to the ocean deoxygenation already under way today. The timing work also carries a counterfactual: in the Burgess reconstruction, the first 300,000 years of Siberian lavas did little damage, and the crisis began only when sills started baking carbon-rich sediments, so had the magma not intruded those volatile-rich basin rocks, the same eruption might have passed with far smaller losses. Without the extinction, the Mesozoic world would have been assembled from a very different and far larger pool of Paleozoic lineages.

beats.action: region.fill { region: siberian-traps-lava-stage-1, anchor: [69.3535, 88.2027], reconstruction: true }
beats.caption: From about 252.24 million years ago, Siberian Traps lavas pour out; roughly two-thirds of the lava erupts over the next 300,000 years, with little effect on the carbon cycle.
At Meishan, carbon isotopes begin to swing toward lighter values about 60,000 years before the die-off: a sign of light carbon entering the ocean and air.
Close to the extinction's onset, eruption gives way to sills spreading through Tunguska Basin sediments; their heat likely releases huge volumes of CO2 and methane.

perspectives.holder: Stanley (2016), PNAS; adopted by the IUGS geoheritage listing
perspectives.account: After subtracting background extinction and removing losses that belong to the earlier end-Guadalupian crisis, about 81% of marine species (80.5–81.5%) and about 62% of genera died out in the terminal Permian event.

perspectives.holder: Earlier rarefaction estimates (Raup 1979; Sepkoski 1986), still widely quoted, e.g. by MIT News in 2015
perspectives.account: Roughly 88–96% of marine species were lost; Stanley argues these figures merged the Guadalupian and end-Permian crises, which were not recognised as separate until 1994.

The base of the Lystrosaurus Assemblage Zone in the Karoo Basin dates to 252.24 ± 0.11 Ma, so the classic terrestrial vertebrate turnover there preceded the marine extinction by over 300,000 years and may have had different causes.

perspectives.holder: Ward et al. (2005); Smith and Botha-Brink (2014), as summarised by Gastaldo et al. (2020)
perspectives.account: Carbon-isotope and magnetic-polarity correlations place the Karoo vertebrate turnover at the same time as the marine crisis, making land and sea losses one event.

perspectives.holder: Burgess and Bowring (2015); Burgess, Muirhead and Bowring (2017)
perspectives.account: Siberian Traps magmatism is a plausible trigger; the extinction coincides with the onset of sill intrusion and contact metamorphism of basin sediments rather than with the earlier lava floods. MIT reported the authors still treat the link as plausible rather than proven.

numbers.label: Duration of the main extinction interval at Meishan (Beds 25–28)
numbers.note: 61 ± 48 kyr (2σ); the abstract rounds to 60 ± 48 kyr. The IUGS listing gives <61 ± 48 kyr.

numbers.label: Marine species lost (Stanley 2016 clustering-adjusted estimate)
numbers.note: Excludes background extinction and the earlier end-Guadalupian event.

numbers.label: Marine species lost (earlier rarefaction estimates, Raup 1979 / Sepkoski 1986)
numbers.note: Reported by Stanley (2016) as inflated by merging two crises; MIT News (2015) still cites ~96%.

numbers.label: Rise in tropical sea-surface temperature across the extinction interval
numbers.note: Approximate: about 23 to 33 °C over the interval per Burgess et al.; Penn et al. (2018) model more than ~10 °C.

numbers.label: Modelled depletion of global marine oxygen
numbers.note: Single model result ('almost 80%'); the press release adds that about half the seafloor became anoxic.

numbers.label: Total volume of Siberian Traps lavas, pyroclastics and intrusions
numbers.note: Consensus range quoted by Burgess & Bowring; published estimates span ~1 to >10 million km³; minimum cumulative ~3 million km³.

numbers.label: Maximum suggested areal extent of the Siberian Traps province
numbers.note: Upper estimate including Taimyr and the West Siberian Basin; Augland et al. argue for adding ~300,000 km² north of Norilsk to the main pulse.

numbers.label: Exposed extent of the Siberian Traps sill complex
numbers.note: >1.5 million km² (Burgess et al. 2017); 1.6 million km² of outcropping Tunguska sills (Augland et al. 2019).

importance.justification: The most severe extinction in the Phanerozoic record, it ends the Paleozoic Era and reshaped all later marine and terrestrial life, so it must be visible at whole-planet view.

aliases.name: Great Dying

reviewer_note: Least sure of the mechanism attribution (sill-driven CO2/CH4 as trigger is the leading but not proven hypothesis) and of the terrestrial-timing debate; the Siberian Traps region pin is the town of Norilsk as a proxy point for a province of up to ~5 million km².
